2.title: About Me
2.content: . Hi my name is Katherine Ellis! . I am a second year PhD student in chemical and biological engineering in the King group. I grew up in Missouri and did my undergrad at the University of Michigan. This past year I was a McCormick DCS and a ChBE local steward and I am passionate about helping my collegues have a better and safeer workplace which is why I am running for CCS! . Please feel free to email me at katell@u.northwestern.edu . Please take a moment to check out my candidate statement and the other talking points and information on this site.

3.title: How will you handle backdues?
3.content: I would make backdues one of my top priorities. My general approach is: prevent them when we can, make the process as easy and transparent as possible, follow up consistently, and treat termination as the absolute last resort after we’ve exhausted other options. First, we should get people signed onto membership cards as early as possible so backdues don’t accumulate in the first place. Second, I’d work closely with the future CCS (Katherine!) to make sure DCSs and local stewards understand the dues situation in their areas/programs and can help with outreach. People are often much more receptive when they’re approached by someone they already know than by the VP suddenly appearing in their inbox. I also want the process to be clearer and less confusing. We should be patient about explaining why dues matter, where the money goes, and how paying dues supports other members when they need the union. I’ve talked with both organizers and rank-and-file members about backdues, and my impression is that most people do understand the principle and are willing to pay when the situation is explained clearly. We should also be honest that our own systems used to be less organized, and recognize that admin-created problems have made some situations unnecessarily complicated. At the same time, I do believe paying dues is part of our responsibility to one another as members. There’s a balance between making things accessible and still treating people like responsible adults. I won’t avoid difficult follow-ups or hard conversations when they’re necessary. As a boxer, I’m not afraid of confrontation, but martial arts also taught me that confrontation usually works best as a last resort, not a first instinct. It might make things even more difficult when people get defensive. So my approach is basically: collaborate, be creative, be persistent, keep following up, and use every reasonable avenue before escalating. But when escalation really is necessary, don’t hesitate to do it. And I also want to give credit to Yara, Maanasa, Katherine, and others who have already been putting a lot of work into improving the backdues system. I’m not assuming this will suddenly become an easy job. I just think the work they’ve already done gives us a stronger foundation, and my job would be to carry that forward and keep making the system better.

5.title: How will you handle backdues?
5.content: By our contract, all members, whether in unit or out of unit, are required to pay dues to NUGW. This is a phenomenal protection that allows our organizing power to thrive while providing all members a say in our union’s decision making. Handling backdues has been a consistent and difficult conversation with stewards and general members alike. Mishandling backdues can cause a member to feel fear and distrust that our union has their best interest at heart. This is why it is vital to approach every conversation with workers who owe backdues with patience and empathy. As the president, I will work hand in hand with the VP of Membership, the CCS, and our steward network to work on organizing plans to reach all workers who owe backdues . To put it plainly, we cannot take shortcuts with backdues enforcement. We all need to put in consistent effort to lay out why we collect dues, what our dues go on to fund, and most importantly, how dues protect us and our coworkers. These conversations should preferably be conducted in person, one-on-one with our coworker to address fears and misconceptions right then and there. The first step in handling backdues is preventing them from accruing in the first place. This comes from an active effort of reaching all workers who have yet to sign cards. We have been consistently working on membership drive and should still be placing heavy emphasis on this practice! . The next step is developing a concrete plan of how to reach members who have slipped through the cracks. This plan should involve heavy steward involvement, which also means that stewards should be bought into the plan as well. Therefore, an organizing plan for reaching these members should be subject to a GMM vote to ensure that all of us are on the same page. Following through with the plan, we must be having consistent and frequent one-on-one conversations with these workers, led with an empathetic lens. In my time, I have found that a majority of members not only want to pay dues, but are excited about the fact that their money is going to a great cause. I believe that we need to approach these workers with that respect and understanding instead of assuming that all those who owe backdues just “don’t want to pay.” There will be cases in which a worker may feel that way, but by assuming all workers who owe back dues just “don’t want to pay dues,” we risk alienating an ally and, by proxy, this vital contract protection in general.

7.title: Based on the bargaining survey, most members would be largely happy with just keeping our contract language as is, making it unlikely that we would have the collective strength needed to get many more protections and benefits in the next contract. Why shouldn’t I consider voting for other candidates because it seems they are heavily folding this assessment into their organizing vision.
7.content: How my perspective differs. I believe that interpretation of the bargaining survey results neglects much of the specific comments left in the survey, overlooks the past three years of grievances and the parts of the contract we still have to fight for today. It has become clear in our organizing through the survey, and in the CAt research groups than on issues surrounding international worker protections, health care and accessibility, and funding security that Northwestern has been able to take advantage of related articles of the contract to harm graduate workers. I also believe from personal experience speaking with many current and incoming workers that these issues are incredibly important to our membership across the university and we can easily gain momentum from them towards the collective strength needed for change. Do you think too much optimism about what we could get in the next contract might be bringing hopes up in only a minority of members without enough power to back it up in time for bargaining? . This is where listening to our membership and empowering them to speak up about the issues they are about becomes extremely important. The more we organize about the issues membership has indicated to us the more likely that optimism will become a reality. At the same time we need to be realistic and emphasize that the contract fight is a negotiation. We need to be asking more specific questions to our members, for example rather than just know what level of priority an issue is we need to know what they would be willing to compromise on in order to save that specific issue. Transparent and open bargaining sessions will also go a long way in helping our membership understand and trust this negotiation process. I want us to be hopeful because hope is powerful, but I also want to make sure we are prepared to deliver on key contract protections in a worse case scenario where Northwestern tries to take away every article we have in our current contract. In other words we need to be optimistic and hope for the best because if we never ask for something we will never get it but we also need to be ready to fight to keep every last article in the contract and know the difference between what our members want and what they cannot survive without. Isn’t this likely to lead to more pain and fracturing in our union down the line? . That is a very realistic concern. If we as a bargaining committee aren’t clear about our priorities going in and if we don’t give membership an explanation for whatever may occur during bargaining then we are sowing the seeds of a divide. If as leadership we want to have the power of our membership behind us for collective bargaining we need to do everything we can to build their trust in us when we sit at the bargaining table. One of the ways I believe we could do this is with open bargaining. Imagine how much understanding membership would have of the contract fight if we let them witness it. If you could watch bargaining sessions then submit a form after with comments on specific articles or what was discussed we as a bargaining committee would know how membership felt before it comes to final contract ratification. Members would be able to trust us because we would be visibly accountable to them during bargaining, helping prevent pain and fracturing in our union down the line. Isn’t it arguably more democratic to heed the sentiment from members that they mostly just want the status quo and just focus on the likely incredibly hard battle of just keeping what we have? . Like I mentioned before, if we never ask for better we will never get anything better. It will be an incredibly hard battle but if keeping what we have now is our bare minimum goal then we must ask for more in our contract, for higher pay, for more protections for international workers, for better healthcare, and we must show that we are willing to fight for a better contract than we have now. We must aim higher because this shows Northwestern that we want better, and then keeping our current status quo becomes the compromise. However if we only ever fight for what we currently have we will be forced to make compromises and end up losing the status quo. We must remember that bargaining is a negotiation and that we have collective bargaining power because Northwestern cannot survive without its graduate workers, and so we must aim higher in the hopes of getting a better contract but prepare for the hard battle that may mean we only keep what’s in our current contract.

9.title: Based on the bargaining survey, most members would be largely happy with just keeping our contract language as is, making it unlikely that we would have the collective strength needed to get many more protections and benefits in the next contract. Optimism is great but do you think too much optimism about what we could get in the next contract might be bringing hopes up in only a minority of members without enough power to back it up in time for bargaining? Isn’t this likely to lead to more pain and fracturing in our union down the line? Isn’t it arguably more democratic to heed the sentiment from members that they mostly just want the status quo and just focus on the likely incredibly hard battle of just keeping what we have?
9.content: Our current contract IS great! The wins of the previous bargaining committee are excellent and I want to ensure that any decision we make will still allow us to protect said wins. However, this does not mean our contract is perfect. For instance, many of our parents feel that the cost of their children’s healthcare is far too high on NU-SHIP. This is something that the University could easily pay for, but they refuse to because the University knows that it can continue to divide us further. As our Accessibility and Healthcare working group has found, parents and caregivers make up only around 2% of the grad student population. But I have and will continue to ask, does that mean we should allow the university to treat them unfairly? Yes, a majority of grad workers are not parents. But, what if we extend that same argument to other inequitably supported groups, do we stop caring for small fractions of the population purely because they aren’t the majority? Absolutely not! The truth is, the University picks on said groups across the University to instill fear that there is no solution for them, which is why we need to speak up for those who the University attempts to silence. This is a win that I do believe is achievable, and the University will try to do everything to make it seem that it is not. But by allowing this thought process to continue, we make it so the University controls the narrative and not us. Being hopeful is not mutually exclusive with being realistic. Yes, the University will most likely attack many of our contract protections. Yes, the University will most likely try and divide us again. Yes, the funding climate in academia right now is atrocious. These are real fears that I and many others have. But these fears cannot stifle us. Fear is a tool used by the University to lull us into inaction. They do this because the University feels that they have power over us. What the University fails to recognize is that they do not. This University works only because the grad workers, staff, and postdocs allow it to. What happens to a class if there is no grad TA for that course? What happens to the University’s grants if there is no grad RA to do the actual day-to-day research? There is a reason why the NLRB decided that PhD students can be labelled as workers, and that is because WE keep these Universities afloat. We have the power at this University, and we cannot let the University strip this power away through these fears. This contract fight will be a hard battle, just as the previous contract was and just as all our future contracts will be. But this is a hard battle that we can, and must, win together. By allowing the University to instill this fear into us, we lose this contract fight before we even begin. If we allow the University to diminish our hopes of what could be, we will lose what we already have. At the end of the day, a new contract can be quite exciting! It is the time in which we can yell at the University and say “I care for my fellow grad workers!” It is the time for us to not only say that we want more protections, but DEMAND that we NEED more protections. Let’s say the University comes after our dental and vision care, do we sit and allow them to take it away? NO! We stand up and fight for it! This fight is a completely different fight, and we need to be prepared for all the stones the University will throw while continuing to push for more. Hope is not the reason why splits occur, it is hope that heals a fractured psyche. There is a better world out there, and we must fight for it.

11.title: Candidate Statement
11.content: Hello! My name is Edward Skrabacz, but you can call me Ed. I am running for President because all workers deserve a fair contract with strong protections, which can only be achieved through our collective power! As President, I want to achieve this by listening to our coworkers and inspiring them to fight for their rights. Throughout my past two years, I have fought alongside my fellow workers to force the university to honor our contract, as well as inspiring other members to speak up along the way. As a Local Steward in Physics and Astronomy and a Divisional Chief Steward for Weinberg STEM, I have advocated for Northwestern to recognize internal fellows and expand our International Employee Support Fund to include passport renewal. Guiding stewards in my own division and beyond has enlightened me to the pressing issues facing workers across Northwestern. As President, I will use these valuable conversations to steer bargaining proposals that reflect the wishes of our membership. In these proposals, I will work to offer greater protections for international workers, to enshrine dependent healthcare for our parents and caregivers, and to force the university to guarantee funding across divisions for the entirety of a worker’s PhD. When I began my PhD here at Northwestern, the striking passion from the workers in NUGW immediately drew me in. At my first meeting, I immediately resonated with the notion that “the members run this union.” As President, this will be my guiding light as I foster a community of open and honest communication where members are unafraid to voice their concerns. It is vital that all members have a say in their next contract, which can be achieved through regularly occurring bargaining updates, steward outreach, and transparency in the bargaining process. By properly fostering connection between all members, we will create a collective force to be reckoned with! . For more information about me and my campaign please visit my campaign website https://katherine-e.github.io/Ed-Yuhan-Katherine-NUGW-Ticket/, or feel free to email me at edward.skrabacz@u.northwestern.edu, I’m always happy to chat :).

12.title: Candidate Statement
12.content: Hi! I’m Katherine (you’re welcome to call me Kate), and I’m running for Campus Chief Steward (CCS) because I am passionate about creating a better and safer work environment for all of us! I believe we are a stronger union when every worker is represented, has a voice, and is empowered to organize around issues they care about most. As CCS, my priorities will be to recruit stewards especially to our underserved divisions; to connect with and energize as many workers as possible to enable transparent, effective, and accessible bargaining; and to educate workers on their rights under our new contract so we can continue our ongoing campaign of grievances. As McCormick Division Chief Steward, I have learned and used the skills I need to make these priorities a reality. I organized around academic discipline and discharge to prevent NU from forcing workers to leave their programs, pursued bargaining-unit exclusion grievances, connected with under organized departments, and built membership participation across my division with 100% of in-unit cards signed each quarter of my term. As CCS, I will fight for transparent and member-driven bargaining. I will listen to the diverse needs of all workers, build a culture of open communication, and support member-led organizing efforts. I will fight to make sure no member is left behind. For more information about me and my campaign please visit my campaign website https://katherine-e.github.io/Ed-Yuhan-Katherine-NUGW-Ticket/ and feel free to contact me via email at katell@u.northwestern.edu .

13.title: Candidate Statement
13.content: Hi, my name is Yuhan Zhang, which means “lotus in the rain,” and stands for integrity in our culture. I am running for Vice President for Membership because I hope to help build a union that is organized, welcoming, and truly shaped by its members. What matters most to me is listening to people with different experiences and understanding what support actually looks like for them. Members should be able to find the information they need, bring forward their own ideas, and have a real say! . 18.title: What are your core values?
18.content: Integrity, Accountability, Balance, and Communication . I want to be accountable for my job and make sure that I am doing my best even when no one is watching. I also know that without balancing workload among each other and ensuring good communication we can’t be good organizers and can’t represent the workers whom we are stewards for.

21.title: Do you have any experience that would help you do well in this role?
21.content: I have been speaking with many past and present stewards and DCSs about what they want to see in the future of their union and in our organizing. These connections and conversations give me incredibly valuable insight to what our elected officers and members want to see and how we as leaders on the executive board can better serve them. I have also spoken to two past campus chief stewards, Peter and Maanasa to learn from their experiences as organizers and CCSs. Their insights on continuing to organize for our underrepresented divisions will set me up to hit the ground running as CCS and make sure that our McCormick and Weinberg divisions are NOT the only ones represented in our contract fight. As I spoke about above I have helped organize what will become the discipline and discharge working group after seeing how prevalent cases have become where administration utilizes loop holes to exclude workers from the bargaining unit and ultimately from their programs. This organizing, its related petitions and grievances that I have been involved with in McCormick protect all workers, especially international students, activists for Palestinian liberation, those who refuse the biased “anti-bias training”, first year student struggling to get placed in labs, workers on leave who need to retain their healthcare, workers facing unfair practices surrounding qualifying exams or prospectus, the list goes on and on. In addition to this organizing I have been part of a push alongside my current co-DCS Pallavi to file list exclusion grievances every quarter and have won several grievances to get Presidential and terminal year fellows in-unit. Pallavi and I have also successfully gotten 100% of in-unit work to sign a member or agency card in winter, spring and fall 2026, and I single handedly made connections to underrepresented departments to achieve this effort. Beyond my experience as a DCS and local steward and the many successful organizing efforts that I helped lead, I also have years of experience running and organizing large organizations. As an undergraduate I was vice president of my professional chemistry fraternity chapter which had almost a hundred active members. Through this leadership experience I became skilled at planning events, member outreach, recruitment, collaboration, communication, and conflict resolution. Additionally in 2022-2023 I was the president of a Michigan state wide youth service organization and was constantly in communication with members to organize fundraising, service events, recruitment, and facilitate connections to our organization in other states.

23.title: Do you have any experience that would help you do well in this role?

25.content: Time as DCS is not necessarily the best indicator for experience. In just six months as McCormick DCS I have helped organize what will become the discipline and discharge working group after seeing how prevalent cases have become where administration utilizes loop holes to exclude workers from the bargaining unit and ultimately from their programs. In addition to this organizing I have been part of a push alongside my current co-DCS Pallavi to file list exclusion grievances every quarter and have won several grievances to get Presidential and terminal year fellows in-unit. Pallavi and I have also successfully gotten 100% of in-unit work to sign a member or agency card in winter, spring and fall 2026, and I single handedly made connections to underrepresented departments to achieve this effort. It is all of these successful and sustained efforts of organizing that I have done as a DCS that make me the best candidate to be CCS. Our workers who deserve a CCS will continue to fight for what matters to them and who will not rest until every single worker is protected, and who will work with every DCS and steward to make sure our organizing is successful, and I believe I have proven I can be that CCS.

27.title: Do you have any experience that would help you do well in this role?

29.title: The constitutional duties of the VP for Membership includes spearheading membership enforcement, which usually requires a lot of listwork and other work that isn’t as “glamorous”/member-facing or immediately gratifying as organizing/activism. Could you speak to any experiences or aptitude you have that would make you well-suited for that type of work?
29.content: I have experience organizing and leading multi-day backpacking trips, where my responsibilities extended well beyond leading the group in the field. I recruited and screened participants, managed surveys and spreadsheets, coordinated logistics, planned routes and itineraries, and prepared the group before departure. What I learned from that experience is that I genuinely enjoy both sides of organizing: the member-facing work and the less visible operational work that makes everything else possible. I am energized by working directly with people, but I also like working with data and information like keeping lists accurate, identifying patterns, following up systematically, and making sure no one falls through the cracks. I have used surveys, spreadsheets, and other tracking systems extensively in both trip organizing and research. For me, those tools are not just administrative tasks; they are a way to understand a group at scale. In a leadership role, it is not realistic to know every member equally well through one-on-one interaction, so good membership data can provide a broader picture of who our members are, where engagement may be dropping off, and where follow-up is needed. That combination of enjoying direct organizing while also being comfortable with detailed, repetitive, behind-the-scenes work is one reason I think I would be well-suited for membership enforcement.

31.title: I haven’t seen you very much before, what has your organizing experience been? Why do you feel you can do this job with only ~5 months organizing experience and no prior EB role? Especially since your opponent is known to be an experienced organizer?
31.content: If we haven’t met or talked much yet, let’s change that!! . I’ve been organizing through DIAS around research, international student orientation, the International Support Fund, and bringing in new international members/organizers while being mindful of their safety. I’ve also made an effort to talk with people leading different areas of union work so I have a good sense of what’s happening beyond just my own projects . I may be newer to union organizing, but I’m not new to leadership. I’ve led other communities and organized multi-day backpacking trips from start to finish which includes recruiting and screening people, planning logistics, managing information, and leading the group in the field (already explained above). I also think being relatively new gives me a useful perspective. My program didn’t have a local steward, so for a long time I experienced the union as a rank-and-file member. When I first got involved, I remember getting sent a ton of documents and folders and thinking, “There has to be an easier way to understand all of this.” I want to make information and onboarding much more accessible, especially for members who are interested but don’t already know how everything works. And VP isn’t a role that stands alone. I’m running as part of a team with Ed and Katherine, who are both respected and experienced organizers, and Yara will be supporting me throughout the transition. We also have many experienced organizers, including people who played major roles in the last contract fight, working alongside us. I plan to listen carefully, learn from that experience, and, honestly, pick everyone’s brains whenever I can lol. I don’t think good leadership means already knowing everything; it means knowing how to bring people together, listen, learn quickly, and make good use of the experience around you.

33.title: You claim to like “healthy disagreement” and a bottom up members based approach to organizing, but how will you actually get things done? What if there is so much discussion about a topic that no choice can be made? In that case, isn’t it better to give the EB a greater amount of authority to make a decision and keep things running?
33.content: Before I answer, I do want to clarify what I mean by “healthy disagreement.” By healthy disagreements, I do not mean allowing for bigotry to foster. Bigotry to me is not a “healthy disagreement” and should not be tolerated or allowed in our spaces. A healthy disagreement to me is one in which both parties hold respect for the other and care for what the other has to say. These disagreements can look like asking for a change of language in a proposal or discussions on how to best run our local. These disagreements do not look like name calling, yelling, general acts of bigotry, or assuming that the other worker is disagreeing in bad faith. With that out of the way, growth only exists when one leaves an area of comfort. As graduate workers, we know full well that learning something new requires you to go against the standard literature and look at others’ work in a new light. Our fields thrive on disruptions, because in these disruptions we learn something new. For example, cool example from physics to get the people pumped. Our organizing power comes from having disagreements with coworkers, and showing Northwestern that these disagreements cannot and will not change the fact that we are stronger together. Our organizing power comes from learning about others’ experiences and navigating conflict together. In having healthy disagreements, and by that I mean disagreements over what policy is best to pass in our local (for example), and by truly listening to one another with an empathetic ear, we can grow alongside one another instead of against. Our organizing power comes from making informed decisions WITH one another. Full discussions on topics are extremely important for all members to make well-informed decisions for the local. While these discussions may be tricky to navigate, I believe that when presented with all of the information in a decision, a majority of members will make the same decision that any EB member would. The duty of the president is to facilitate these decisions, such that all voices are heard and membership can make this well-informed decision. If no decision gets made, it is because the discussions were not made beforehand. If further discussion on a topic is needed, then that discussion should continue. For our union to remain strong, members need to own the decisions being made. Giving EB a greater amount of authority may seem appealing, after all we voted them in, but the EB is still a small population in comparison to the entire local. The executive board’s role in our union is not to alleviate the decision making capabilities from general members. Instead, the executive board’s role is to communicate with members about what the people across our university desire to see and act on that. This only happens if the president, the executive board, and general members are willing to have a discussion where members feel comfortable to voice their opinion.

35.title: There has been significant discussion, both during the last contract cycle and leading into the current one, about how members’ voices should be incorporated into the bargaining process. What is your vision for how members can learn about and provide feedback into the course of bargaining? Will the opinions of those in and out of the BU be considered differently? What does rank-and-file democracy look like between the time that the BC is elected and the contact is voted on?
35.content: . | Weekly bargaining updates: proposals, admin responses, movement, and unresolved issues. | Short issue-specific surveys before major bargaining decisions. | Stewards/DCSs bring department-level feedback directly back to the BC. | Town halls at major turning points, especially before dropping or trading major demands. | Anonymous feedback option for members who do not want to speak publicly. | Targeted outreach to less-engaged departments/groups, not just people already active in union spaces. | BU members have decision-making priority; non-BU workers can still provide relevant input and context. | Publish what we heard from members so surveys and meetings do not feel like a black box. | . These are methods for these things, and as leaders, it’s important to keep up with them and make sure the people responsible are doing the same. It’s much easier to add meeting notes to the folder as you go than to sort through a big pile of documents later. But most importantly, I don’t think our role should just be keeping members informed and in the loop. We also need to get people excited, encourage them to take action, and support them in fighting for what they believe in. We should give people a platform to speak up and take initiative. It’s always more powerful when people feel like they are making things happen, rather than just hearing about what has already happened.

37.title: There has been significant discussion, both during the last contract cycle and leading into the current one, about how members’ voices should be incorporated into the bargaining process. What is your vision for how members can learn about and provide feedback into the course of bargaining? Will the opinions of those in and out of the BU be considered differently? What does rank-and-file democracy look like between the time that the BC is elected and the contact is voted on?
37.content: I believe that member’s voices should be at the forefront of the bargaining process. Part of this comes from direct communication to and from the bargaining committee in consistent bargaining updates and an easily accessible bargaining tracker. While these tools are exceptionally helpful to learn about what is happening at the bargaining table, we must also allow for members to be involved in the drafting and editing of proposed articles. By allowing members to assist in the drafting process, we both show that the BC is acting in accordance with members’ wishes and members develop a stronger bond to the contract itself. To paraphrase Alexandra Bradburry, there are no “ins and outs” if everyone feels like they were “in” from the start. To reach all members, we must use our steward network to ask for targeted feedback on specific proposals both before general membership meetings and before the BC presents said proposals at the bargaining table. Once the stewards learn what membership wants, they should bring their findings directly to the BC where the proposal will then be edited in accordance with members’ wishes. These proposals could be shown to membership through outreach such as walkthroughs, anonymous feedback forms, town halls, suggesting access on copies of proposal documents, or a combination of everything before. Outside of drafting proposal documents, members can also decide whether to have bargaining sessions open to general members, which can be an extremely powerful tool for many reasons: . 1) Open bargaining shows members that the BC is acting on their behalf and shows the BC that the members have their backs, and in doing so we build solidarity 2) Open bargaining allows members to see the university’s shady tactics directly, and in doing so we build our power 3) Open bargaining shows the university that we all are watching, and in doing so we show our strength . However, the university could become less likely or unwilling to speak on compromises at the bargaining table if this occurs for every session. In contrast, this also means that the university may be less willing to attempt a ruthless attack on our contract, which could be very vital in this current political climate. Open bargaining could also cause bargaining to become a slower process, which in our much shorter bargaining timeline could become quite the hassle. With more people in the room, there will be more voices that can be heard. However, just as our GMMs follow Robert’s Rules of Order, we can establish similar practices during an open bargaining session to allow for proper time management. With all this being said, I am by no means an expert on this topic either, and I will push for a more fruitful discussion with BC and membership should be had before we begin bargaining. In terms of bargaining unit status, we are forced into difficult conversations based on the bad practices of Northwestern University. Famously, the university tends to overwhelmingly consider Humanities and Social Studies workers out of the bargaining unit while STEM workers tend to be considered in unit. This is completely bad practice from the university and should be treated as such. All grad workers at Northwestern are working for Northwestern and deserve to be protected by our contract. We must not forget that this distinction only exists because the university arbitrarily decided to place people off the bargaining unit and we must continue to fight to include more workers to be formally recognized. To me, the members must feel like they have control over the contract to feel like it is truly theirs. By doing extended outreach to members both in and out of the grievance table, we can maintain our current protections AND fight for protections that are even greater! .

39.title: Other candidates seem like they would be a great President again because they have a lot of passion for unions, including reading several works on labor history in their spare time to have a strong foundation on labor theory and NUGW-UE’s broader context in the labor movement. I’m worried about the idea of voting for a President who doesn’t have a deep knowledge of our labor history.
39.content: There are many ways in which one can learn how to organize, including reading theory. However, theory and application are two vastly different skill sets. As a physics PhD worker, I have learned the theories of quantum mechanics, but that doesn’t inherently imply that I can operate a scanning tunneling microscope. In my own experience organizing, I have learned from some of our best organizers and have experienced first hand how to effectively alleviate people’s fears and frustrations of organizing and turning that into actionable items. Alongside that, I do agree that a bit of knowledge on labor theory does help organizers develop guiding principles for which they can stand by, which is why I do read labor theory in my free time as well. In terms of NUGW-UE’s broader context in the labor movement, we have the power to shape this story together through both communications in our union and our sibling locals such as Chicago GSU. I also know that in places where I may falter (such as a deep, sophisticated study of the labor movement), I can rely on my fellow organizers who actively study labor movements for their PhD to bring that knowledge and context to the forefront of our struggle. Labor history and knowledge is built on the work of millions who have come before me, which is why I plan on having consistent communications with organizers across our local and at other locals to develop new paths forward in solidarity.

41.title: In the eyes of the Boss and the government, humanities & social science research has been far more undervalued than STEM research. Why should I vote for a STEM Campus Chief Steward instead of a H/SS Campus Chief Steward who would better represent this population of more vulnerable graduate workers?
41.content: The undervaluing of the humanities and social sciences, especially in recent years, has been absurdly frustrating to see. As a STEM researcher, I cannot say that I have experienced the same level of attacks that people in the humanities and social sciences have. But, I have and will continue to learn about how these attacks disproportionately affect studies besides my own. I have talked with many in the humanities and social sciences to learn about how the University weaponizes contract protections like bargaining unit status to deny humanities and social science researchers access to contract protections, 6th/7th year funding, and the international worker support fund. These denials are completely unjust, and I hope to continue fighting for and learning from humanities and social science researchers to give everyone the protections that they rightfully deserve as employees of Northwestern. I believe that all people should have a balance between science and the humanities. This divide between STEM and the humanities has been intentionally placed to cause each group to discredit the other, but it is a distraction. This divide is a distraction that is meant to cause us to lose faith in the other instead of fighting for what is best for the other. As president, I hope to end this divide and help all grad workers recognize that when the university attacks one area of research, they attack all areas of research.

43.title: Do you feel that as an international worker and all the burdens that come with that,  you will be able to perform your duties as VP?
43.content: Most people I’ve talked to see my international background as a strength, though I’m also aware of the risk of being tokenized. Everyone is carrying struggles that other people may not see, and that’s part of why we organize: we understand, empathize, and stand together. As an international graduate worker and organizer, I personally know the stress, uncertainty, and extra burdens that many international workers live with. That doesn’t make me less able to do this job. It’s actually one of the biggest reasons I want to do it. I want other people to have to carry less of that fear and uncertainty than I have. At the same time, I don’t assume my experience represents every international worker. Our situations can be very different. My job is to listen, collect information, make sure different groups have space to speak for themselves, and help turn those different needs into collective action for better protections and benefits. Of course, this doesn’t mean I would only advocate for international students’ rights and benefits. I want to hear from and work with all workers. We all deserve a dignified, protected workplace.

44.title: In the eyes of the Boss and the government, humanities & social science research has been far more undervalued than STEM research. Why should I vote for a STEM Campus Chief Steward instead of a H/SS Campus Chief Steward who would better represent this population of more vulnerable graduate workers?
44.content: As I said above I believe a large part of my job as CCS is listening to others, listening to our workers, listening to our stewards, listening to our DCSs, and even more importantly creating an environment of trust where our workers feel empowered to share their voice and their perspective. This also means making sure that we don’t allow our union to reflect the attitude of the Boss and the government and undervalue our non-STEM workers. As a woman in a career built for men I understand how it feels to be underestimated and undervalued and I never want to make any of my fellow workers at Northwestern feel that way. I refuse to be a CCS who lets the Boss and government dictate which of our workers matter, because they ALL matter and we as a union cannot use our collective power without ALL workers.

62.title: What is your vision for the next year?
62.content: Next year will involve three big focuses as CCS, they are not completely separate and build upon each other.  . First, we must recruit and elect new stewards ahead of our bargaining fight. This means reaching workers who may be interested but also communicating with them about how to be a steward and why, especially this year, having stewards in as many departments as possible is more important than ever. This starts to lay the organizing framework we will need during our contract fight and even if we don’t find stewards for every department we must make contacts in every department. I also envision working heavily with the new DCSs and existing stewards to accomplish this as they will know their divisions more intimately than I do and will be our most effective tools in reaching workers and new stewards. Secondly we must be organized for and during our contract fight. I envision that this will entail utilizing those contacts we made while recruiting stewards to hear what our members care about. Our bargaining will need to be as transparent as possible to membership because that is what they deserve. I see CCS as the information conduit for this transparency. I must work with DCSs to make sure as stewards we are speaking directly to workers, that no concern is being overlooked and no one feels silenced or underrepresented. I must also make sure this information is getting to the BC through myself and the DCSs. Having membership input will never be useful unless we are listening to it and having bargaining information be available isn’t useful unless we are making sure its accessible to our workers. Thirdly, we must continue our campaigns of grievances whether it be for unit exclusions, discipline and discharge, or any other issue our workers are facing. Not only are grievances an opportunity to protect and empower workers but they are critical evidence at the bargaining table and prove to administration that we will not give up on fighting for our workers just because bargaining is around the corner. Then after we have our new contract we must make it as easy to understand for members as possible, this includes holding town halls, training, communications, info graphics and flyers. Workers deserve to know their rights under the contract so that they can know when to file a grievance if that contract is violated. I envision this will involve much collaboration between myself, the grievance committee and stewards so we can continue to use our organizing skills to protect workers under their contract.

72.title: Why do you want to run for this role?
72.content: I want to be Campus Chief Steward because I believe I have the skills and motivation to use this role to continue helping workers across our union. I know first hand how important it is to listen to our workers, to empower them and their voices, and to support them in organizing around key issues. I have also seen how issues that may seem isolated to a specific division like discipline and discharge are important across the entire university and I want to enable our union to make those connections so we can utilize experiences in one division to help workers in another. I also know how hard the job of our executive board and bargaining committee is and how hard it can be being a local steward. I believe I can foster a supportive community that enables our stewards to be the best organizers they can be. I want to be CCS because I think I could do a good job and am willing to listen to constructive input from those around me to build a better union and work environment at Northwestern for us all.

74.title: Experienced UE negotiators like Kim Lawson provided instrumental guidance to the first BC, helping us win an exceptionally strong first contract (especially compared to the first contracts of peer unions like UIC). What’s so wrong about voting for other candidates who have a strong track record of heeding advice from UE organizers and/or GEB?
74.content: To be honest, I don’t think there’s anything wrong with voting for any candidate. Voting for candidate A doesn’t mean candidate B is necessarily incompetent. People come in with different beliefs and priorities, and candidates are always going to be different. It’s our job to explain what we believe in clearly, and may the person who best represents what most members want win. I’ve talked with a lot of organizers who were involved in the last contract fight, and I do think saying “UE helped us win an exceptionally strong first contract” can be a little misleading if it leaves out the enormous amount of work done by our own local organizers. UE staff have provided important guidance and resources, but our members and organizers were the ones who built the campaign, made decisions, mobilized workers, and fought for that contract. I think any advice (or even instruction) that comes from outside should remain neutral. Yes, we are a UE local, but first and foremost, NUGW is a member-run union. We should always believe that our members know best what they want and need, and that our own workers know best how to fight for those things. I absolutely agree that we need to stand in solidarity with existing groups on campus, like postdocs, undergraduates, non-tenure-track faculty, etc., and make full use of all the support and resources available to us during a contract fight, including help from UE staff. But all of that needs to be built on the basis that WE are taking the initiative and ownership, that we represent the rights and needs of graduate workers in our local, and that this principle is respected by everyone we work with.

76.title: Experienced UE negotiators like Kim Lawson provided instrumental guidance to the first BC, helping us win an exceptionally strong first contract (especially compared to the first contracts of peer unions like UIC). What’s so wrong about voting for other candidates who have a strong track record of heeding advice from UE organizers and/or GEB?
76.content: UEs advice and aid was vital in our first contract fight, and will prove vital again. However since that first contract fight we have gained an immense amount of organizing experience, bargaining experience, and an intimate knowledge of what our members need. UE negotiators are not grad students living the day to day of our Northwestern workers, and while their experience is valuable we as an executive board must be willing to stand up for our workers when UEs advice does not reflect what our workers need or our experience as a local. So yes while we will need the strength and support of UE we have to be able to always put our workers first.

78.title: Experienced UE negotiators like Kim Lawson provided instrumental guidance to the first BC, helping us win an exceptionally strong first contract (especially compared to the first contracts of peer unions like UIC). What’s so wrong about voting for other candidates who have a strong track record of heeding advice from UE organizers and/or GEB?
78.content: As our parent union, UE provides all of us with said instrumental guidance, not just Theo or Amanda. I believe that we should continue to have conversations with UE negotiators due to their many years of experience as well. However, it is important to recognize that the first contract was not won just because of the UE negotiators. Our strong first contract was won due to members like you participating and organizing alongside your peers. Our first contract was won because of a substantial effort done by our members. While UE’s guidance has greatly assisted our organizing capacity, we must also ensure that we are heeding the wishes of our membership first and foremost. As president, it will be my duty to understand UE’s suggestions as well as membership’s and make the choice that works best for our local, while maintaining the members’ wishes come first. Aside from that, I am very excited to work, to learn, and to organize with Alex and Sofia, who have both already shown the same passion and core values that we all have as well! .

84.doc: Why I'm Not Running On A Slate
84.title: Why are you choosing to not run with a slate? Don’t you think that going into the election with a full slate shows a level of commitment and shared values and ideals, and shows that the EB will function as a cohesive unit?
84.content: I believe that in NUGW, we all want what is best for our local. The differences we have are mainly in how we achieve those. While I put my trust in the others I am running with, I still believe that slates inherently cause one question that bothers me. What happens if all elections are unopposed except for one? There becomes an inherent advantage in being a part of the slate, and the opposing candidate inherently becomes an “outsider.” But what if that “outsider” would bring in some fantastic ideas that no one on the slate had thought of before? Does this discredit the slate? In my opinion, it shouldn’t discredit the slate, but on a glance it could. I am opposed to the notion that this “outsider” is even an outsider at all. We are all just people trying to fight for what we believe to be good for our union. Call me optimistic (which I still fail to see how this is a bad thing), but I also do believe that our organizers and our members do have a similar set of shared values and ideals, and I remain unwilling to treat others in a way that shows otherwise. The commitment to a slate, at least to me, removes the idea that elections should remain on a personal basis. I will, of course, back those who I believe to be best for this union and campaign with them, but I also trust that membership has the final say in any decision that is made for our union. So, I am running without a slate to allow membership to make well-informed decisions with no prior bias that could be established through a slate’s implementation.

86.doc: Why am I Suited to the Role of President?
86.title: The President role is one of the most difficult and intense roles of the LEB and has a steep learning curve. Why do you think you’d be better-suited for the role than the incumbent? This is a bargaining year. Why would I take a risk on someone new if the incumbent is already doing a fine job?
86.content: One of the largest duties of the president is to ensure that all members of our union feel heard and understood. Nearly all of the time, this comes from one-on-one conversations with stewards and general members across all departments to truly understand how issues affect all workers. From these conversations, the president has the ability to alleviate fear and inspire the stewards and members to take action on their own. In my time as DCS, I encouraged many local stewards to pursue grievances and actions that became crucial for the organizing of our upcoming contract. For instance, I heavily encouraged many stewards in DIAS to pursue the passport renewal grievance, which made it all the way to Level 3 and won! The majority of the work was not done by me, but by giving guidance and inspiring hope into our local organizers. By passing along my knowledge and experience to newer organizers, we were able to work together to win this grievance. In this way, I was able to play a crucial role in expanding this protection from our contract and I will continue to assist and support newer organizers so that we can have a strong union of confident organizers. I also assisted our local organizers in the expansion of the Accessibility and Healthcare working group, which has done the excellent work of organizing around our current and future healthcare protections. This work has done a tremendous amount of good for our union, including “Know Your Healthcare” workshops that have been useful for members across the university. This working group has also paved the way to enshrine dependent healthcare into our contract for our parents and caregivers. I am not the lead of this working group. Instead, I have been a participant who only hoped to see that others were becoming more involved. I have also been at the grievance table for my workers many times as both DCS and as a local steward. I have won fights on recognition of internal fellows (including, but not limited to, Presidential and John M Nicholson Fellows) and continue to fight for TAs in the math department who have actively been denied contract protections, such as their protection to work during normal work hours. I have fought for workers who have been threatened with academic discipline and discharge. While some of these fights were ultimately unsuccessful, I continue to learn from these experiences on how we can continue forcing the university to honor the protections we mutually agreed upon. For years, I have regularly attended the Organizing Committee, Contract Action Team, and GMMs to learn from other organizers and take action for myself. I have admittedly missed some of these meetings that I wish I had not, but I have always been committed to staying informed through meeting minutes and conversations with peers and fellow organizers. I believe that a lot of our current organizing power has been focused on telling a steward or member to do something as opposed to asking them if they are willing to. In the upcoming contract fight, I envision a union where we truly understand members’ fears and concerns with the potential of a strike. We need to deeply understand these workers so that they feel confident in said strike. Without the buy-in of membership, we do not have the organizing power we need. To get that buy-in, we cannot simply tell the members to strike, we must ask why they would not and show them that the people of this university have the true power. I believe that I have the capability of fostering such an environment for our union. Most of all, I believe I am best for this role as I have an unblinding faith in my fellow organizers and general membership that will never falter. All of us are a part of this union for a reason: we all work to protect each other. That means that the work we do is done together. I have trust that all of us want to put in the work to ensure this union runs properly. Much of the duty of the president is delegation and ensuring that the work gets done.

90.doc: Why am I the best candidate for this role?
90.title: Why do you think you’re the best for the role and what experience do you have to help you do well in this role?
90.content: I believe I am the best choice for campus chief steward because I have a track record of organizing around the issues our workers care about most. I have helped organize what will become the discipline and discharge working group after seeing how prevalent cases have become where administration utilizes loop holes to exclude workers from the bargaining unit and ultimately from their programs. This organizing, its related petitions and grievances that I have been involved with in McCormick protect all workers, especially international students, activists for Palestinian liberation, those who refuse the biased “anti-bias training”, first year student struggling to get placed in labs, workers on leave who need to retain their healthcare, workers facing unfair practices surrounding qualifying exams or prospectus, the list goes on and on. In addition to this organizing I have been part of a push alongside my current co-DCS Pallavi to file list exclusion grievances every quarter and have won several grievances to get Presidential and terminal year fellows in-unit. Pallavi and I have also successfully gotten 100% of in-unit workers to sign a member or agency card in winter, spring and summer 2026, and I single handedly made connections to underrepresented departments to achieve this effort. It is all of these successful and sustained efforts of organizing that I have done as a DCS that make me the best candidate to be CCS. Our workers who deserve a CCS will continue to fight for what matters to them and who will not rest until every single worker is protected, and who will work with every DCS and steward to make sure our organizing is successful, and I believe I can be that CCS.
